title: Forecast the Weather, Not the Price — gating models by tradeability
thesis: Open candlestick foundation models like Kronos give you a forecast on every bar, and a hedge-fund stress test says it fails on many levels. A separate save shows the better question: a small logistic regression that predicts tomorrow's efficiency ratio (trend versus chop) and skips the choppy days lifted almost every metric over two years out of sample. Physics-flavored measures in the quant collection — Lempel-Ziv compressibility, Hurst exponent, Lyapunov exponent, hidden Markov regimes — are all measures of the same thing: is this market forecastable right now? Use them as a confidence gate on the foundation model, not as signals.
why_it_matters: You stop asking a model to be right everywhere and only ask it to be right where structure exists. That turns a free open model plus a few cheap statistics into something you can actually size positions with.
action_sketch:
Run Kronos zero-shot on two years of hourly BTC and QQQ and log every forecast with its realized error.
Compute rolling efficiency ratio, Lempel-Ziv complexity and Hurst for each bar, bucket bars into tradeability quintiles, and plot Kronos error per quintile.
If error falls across quintiles, fit the efficiency-ratio-style logistic model to predict next-period tradeability and paper-trade Kronos only in the top bucket.
falsifier: if Kronos error is flat across tradeability quintiles, the complexity measures say nothing about this model's skill and the gate is decoration.

entries.transcript: I built a machine learning model that predicts how the market will move. It improved almost every performance metric on one of my strategies. Instead of trying to predict direction, the model predicts the next day's efficiency ratio. The efficiency ratio basically measures how efficiently price moves in one direction. A high ratio means price moved clean in one direction while a low ratio means price chopped back and forth. The model makes its predictions with a logistic regression that weights 15 different measurements of how price has been moving. To see if these predictions actually mean anything, I took one of my strategies and I split each trade based off what the model predicted. And the difference was pretty clear. High efficiency days performed the best while the low efficiency days made about a third of the money per trade. So I added a gate that skips those low efficiency days entirely, and that one change improved almost every performance metric. And more importantly, that improvement held on two years of data the model's never seen. If you want to see what this model predicts every day, comment model and I'll send it to you.

title: Scan, Fit, Print — agents that design parts around real objects
thesis: Open-source scanners (a smartphone Orbiter rig, a Raspberry Pi handheld LiDAR, LingBot-Map's video-to-3D) now produce a usable mesh of the thing you need to fit. LLMs already write Blender Python, and they can build a CLI for any app that has no MCP. Point the agent at the scan, have it write parametric CAD that references the scanned surfaces, and you get a custom-fit part on the first print. That is the step generative 3D can't do yet.
why_it_matters: Makers, repair people and small product designers spend most of their CAD time measuring and re-printing. Tolerance-aware agent CAD collapses the loop from 'calipers, sketch, print, fail, repeat' into 'scan, describe, print'. Y-Pan and Gemma Translator show that whole working devices ship as STL plus a bill of materials.
action_sketch:
Scan three awkward real objects (a tool handle, a bike mount point, a phone in its case) with the Orbiter workflow or photogrammetry; export clean meshes.
Have Claude Code write a CadQuery/FreeCAD script that imports the mesh, fits planes/cylinders to the contact surfaces, and builds a mount with a stated clearance (e.g. 0.3 mm); prompt it to build its own CLI for the slicer.
Print, test fit, feed caliper measurements back as corrections; log iterations-to-fit for agent vs your hand CAD.
Falsifier: if agent CAD needs more print iterations than your own hand CAD on 3 of 3 objects, the scan-to-parametric step isn't ready — the fitting step, not the scanner, is the bottleneck.
prerequisites: Phone camera or Pi + LiDAR module
Claude Code or similar coding agent

title: Benchmark Your Brain — the skill-optimizer loop, pointed at the human
thesis: The agent world now rewrites skills against benchmarks: SkillOpt rejects any edit that doesn't beat the eval, Karpathy-style autoresearch adds an outer coach loop, and skills log their own failures for batch rewrites. Meanwhile the catalog's learning entries stop at 'turn saves into quizzes'. Run the same loop on yourself. Your saves are the training set, auto-generated quizzes are the eval set, and an outer coach rewrites your study playbook whenever your scores plateau.
why_it_matters: Most people's save folders are graveyards, and this catalog is one. Closing the loop turns passive saving into measured skill gain, and it reports which topics never stick, so you can drop or re-approach them. The same harness already works for agents, so the build is small.
action_sketch:
Export the last 60 days of saves (DejaViewed parquet works) into a table; a weekly Claude skill clusters them into 3 topics and writes 15 retrieval questions each, held out from the study notes.
Quiz yourself cold, log scores per topic; the coach skill rewrites the study playbook (spacing, format: explain-back, build-a-thing, game) only if next week's held-out score beats the last.
Add chat-history mining monthly: questions you re-asked the AI become forced quiz items.
Falsifier: if held-out scores after 6 weeks are no better than a no-coach control topic studied with plain flashcards, the outer loop adds overhead not learning.

entries.title: Bilevel autoresearch loops — an outer coach loop rewrites the search
entries.summary: Builds on Karpathy's autoresearch loop (try change, test, keep or revert). An outer coach loop watches the inner worker and rewrites its search playbook so it stops repeating the same ideas; claimed ~5x better on Karpathy's benchmark with the same models.

entries.caption: How to 5x your loop system with Bilevel loops #ai #tech
entries.transcript: Most people don't realize that you can get 5x more efficiency from a loop system by just adding another loop on top. Here's how the bi-level loop system works. If you don't already, Andre Carpethy, one of the co-founders of OpenAI, released a loop engineering system that works when you give AI a goal and it works towards it by itself. It tries to change and test whether the results get better. Keeps it if it did, throws a weight if it didn't, and tries the next idea all automated. But here's a problem nobody noticed. Even good loops have bad habits. AI has instincts about what kinds of ideas to try. It keeps going back over the same instincts over and over even after they stop working. Your loop runs 500 experience, but it's really running the same 10 ideas 50 times. This is a fix that Frontier Lab scientists found out. You just add a second loop on top of the first one. The inner loop is the worker. It keeps running experiments exactly like before while the top loop is the coach. The coach does not do any of the work. Its only job is to watch the worker. The coach in the outer loop rewrites the worker's playbook, changing the way it searches for ideas and then setting it back in. Researchers tested this on the same exact benchmark that Carpethy used, and this new Tula version scored five times better than a single loop with the same exact LLM models. The entire improvement came from the structure that one AI is forcing the other AI to explore ideas that normally its instincts would have skipped. I created a step-by-step guide on how to build out a bi-level loop system within your current loop. If you want it, just like the video and comment level and I'll send it to you. title: Mission Control for 80 Agents — Conway's law meets game UI
thesis: Once you run more than a handful of agents, the bottleneck is your attention, not tokens. Feed a Booking.com-style trace bus into a game-engine front end and you get a control room where structure is visible.
why_it_matters: Solo operators running Founder-OS-style setups spend their day polling terminals. A spatial view that surfaces only blocked agents, and whose layout mirrors how work is partitioned, lets one person supervise ten times more agents without reading every log.

entries.transcript: In 1967, a computer scientist called Melvin Conway noticed something strange enough that he wrote it up and sent it to Harvard Business Review. They rejected it on the grounds that he hadn't proved his thesis, so he sent it to a computing magazine instead, and they published it in 68. And the idea became one of the most quietly confirmed observations in how organizations work. Any company that designs a system will produce a design that copies the company's own communication structure, not as a metaphor, but literally. Four teams building a compiler will ship a compiler with four parts. A company where two departments barely speak will ship a product where two components barely connect. The organization chart leaks into the product piece by piece, whether anyone intends it or not. I told the Sony story a while ago, three divisions invading incompatible music players on the same stage, and Conway is the law underneath it. The customer ends up holding a physical copy of your internal politics. The reason is almost obvious, once said out loud. People design what they can talk about, and they can only talk across the channels that exist. If the channel between two teams is thin, the connection between their two components will be also thin and awkward and late. The lens that follows is the sharp part, and modern engineering systems and teams use it deliberately. Design the organization for the product you want, because you're going to ship your organization chart either way. So look at your own product honestly. Which gap in it is actually a gap between two of your teams?

entries.title: Shepherd dog flock simulation — pressure-field + boids rules
entries.summary: @simulateitnow explains a flock-herding simulation combining a pressure-field force F=(1-d/R)^1.2 with classic boids (cohesion/alignment/separation). Great reference for swarm/multi-agent simulation math.
entries.creator: simulateitnow
entries.caption:
A single shepherd dog can control an entire flock of sheep without ever touching them. The secret is spatial pressure — the exploitation of every prey animal's flight zone.
When a predator (or herding dog) enters the flight zone — the minimum distance at which an animal perceives a threat — the animal moves away. The dog does not chase individual sheep. Instead, it positions itself behind the flock relative to the target destination. This creates a directional pressure wave that pushes the entire group forward.
The pressure force follows an inverse-distance relationship: F = (1 − d/R)^1.2, where R is the pressure radius. Sheep closer to the dog flee harder. Sheep at the edge barely react. Th
entries.transcript: A single dog controls 60 sheep without any commands. It uses nothing but spatial pressure. The pressure radius defines the zone. Everything inside that circle moves away from the dog. A wider radius means the dog controls more sheep at once. Total flock control. Shrink the radius and the dog must chase harder. The sheep scatter in every direction. Cohesion is the glue holding the flock together. It determines how tightly they pack. High cohesion and the flock moves as a single dense ball. One unit easy to herd. Low cohesion and individuals break away. Total chaos for the dog. Stubborn sheep resist the dog's pressure. They refuse to flee as easily. Maximum stubbornness and sheep plant their feet. They barely move even when pressured. Zero stubbornness and they are completely docile. The dog herds them effortlessly. Now a faster dog. Watch what happens when we increase the speed. The dog covers the entire field. No sheep escapes its reach. Real shepherd dogs use these exact pressure mechanics every day. This is how it works. entries.summary: Ian Hubert shows physics-driven vehicle animation in Blender: active/passive rigid bodies, hinge and spring constraints, motor constraints pushing against the ground as thrusters, gravity off, and custom properties wired via drivers with scripted expressions for throttle and lights. takeaways: A linear motor constrained to an immovable object acts like a thruster
